arch.merchant.obsession: Follow the monsoon; weave a net across the ocean.
arch.polo.name: A traveller in Polo’s manner
arch.polo.obsession: Go east, and reach the Kaan’s court.
arch.steppe.name: The steppe road
arch.steppe.obsession: Cross the grass, and see the Kaan’s tents.

city.zayton.market.desc: The quay of Zayton runs the length of the water and is never quiet. Pepper comes ashore in sacks the height of a man; there are pearls weighed out in little brass scales, and lignaloes and sandalwood stacked like cordwood. You must know that the merchant pays dearly here: the Kaan takes a tamghā on everything, ten in the hundred, and the ship's charge on top of it — thirty in the hundred on small wares, forty on bulky goods, and four and forty on pepper. Between the freight and the Kaan's due a man pays out a good half of what his cargo is worth. And yet on the other half he makes so great a profit that he is always glad to come back with more.
city.zayton.market.name: The Quay at Zayton
city.zayton.name: Zayton
city.zayton.shrine.desc: Above the anchorage, on a hill that catches the first light off the sea, stands the temple of the sea-goddess. Her gilded image faces south over the water; at her feet lie the offerings of shipmasters — paper burnt, rice set out, a cup of wine. No master of this coast puts out without going up to her first, and none of them calls it fortune-telling. They call it asking.
city.zayton.shrine.name: The Temple of the Sea
city.zayton.wonder: You have heard men speak of Alexandria and her hundred spired warehouses. Know this: for every shipload of pepper that reaches Alexandria bound for Christendom, a hundred such come in to this haven of Zayton — aye, and more too. The ships of India crowd the water so thickly that their masts, seen from the hill at sunrise, look like a burnt forest. And it is not only pepper. Precious stones, pearls, spicery of every kind that grows, silk enough to clothe an empire — all of it passes through this quay, and the Kaan's clerks are not finished counting before the next season's fleet appears on the horizon.
codex.cx-aden.body: You must know that in the province of ADEN there is a Prince who is called the Soldan. The people are all Saracens and adorers of Mahommet, and have a great hatred of Christians. There are many towns and villages in the country.
codex.cx-aden.name: Aden
codex.cx-badashan.body: Badashan is a Province inhabited by people who worship Mahommet, and have a peculiar language. It forms a very great kingdom, and the royalty is hereditary. All those of the royal blood are descended from King Alexander and the daughter of King Darius, who was Lord of the vast Empire of Persia.
codex.cx-badashan.name: Badashan
codex.cx-balc.body: Balc is a noble city and a great, though it was much greater in former days. But the Tartars and other nations have greatly ravaged and destroyed it. There were formerly many fine palaces and buildings of marble, and the ruins of them still remain.
codex.cx-balc.name: Balc
codex.cx-baldacum.body: Baudas is a great city, which used to be the seat of the Calif of all the Saracens in the world, just as Rome is the seat of the Pope of all the Christians. A very great river flows through the city, and by this you can descend to the Sea of India.
codex.cx-baldacum.name: Baudas
codex.cx-cacanfu.body: Cacanfu is a noble city. The people are Idolaters and burn their dead; they have paper-money, and live by trade and handicrafts. For they have plenty of silk from which they weave stuffs of silk and gold, and sendals in large quantities.
codex.cx-cacanfu.name: Cacanfu
codex.cx-cachanfu.body: When you leave the castle, and travel about 20 miles westward, you come to a river called CARAMORAN, so big that no bridge can be thrown across it; for it is of immense width and depth, and reaches to the Great Ocean that encircles the Universe,—I mean the whole earth.
codex.cx-cachanfu.name: Cachanfu
codex.cx-caiju.body: Caiju is a small city towards the south-east. The people are subject to the Great Kaan and have paper-money. It stands upon the river before mentioned. At this place are collected great quantities of corn and rice to be transported to the great city of Cambaluc for the use of the Kaan’s Court;
codex.cx-caiju.name: Caiju
codex.cx-cail.body: Cail is a great and noble city, and belongs to ASHAR, the eldest of the five brother Kings. It is at this city that all the ships touch that come from the west, as from Hormos and from Kis and from Aden, and all Arabia, laden with horses and with other things for sale.
codex.cx-cail.name: Cail
codex.cx-calatu.body: Calatu is a great city, within a gulf which bears the name of the Gulf of Calatu. It is a noble city, and lies 600 miles from Dufar towards the north-west, upon the sea-shore. The people are Saracens, and are subject to Hormos.
codex.cx-calatu.name: Calatu
codex.cx-camadi.body: After you have ridden down hill those two days, you find yourself in a vast plain, and at the beginning thereof there is a city called CAMADI, which formerly was a great and noble place, but now is of little consequence, for the Tartars in their incursions have several times ravaged it.
codex.cx-camadi.name: Camadi
codex.cx-cambaet.body: Cambaet is a great kingdom lying further west. The people are Idolaters, and have a language of their own, and a king of their own, and are tributary to nobody. The North Star is here still more clearly visible; and henceforward the further you go west the higher you see it.
codex.cx-cambaet.name: Cambaet
codex.cx-cambaluc.body: You must know that the city of Cambaluc hath such a multitude of houses, and such a vast population inside the walls and outside, that it seems quite past all possibility. There is a suburb outside each of the gates, which are twelve in number;
codex.cx-cambaluc.name: Cambaluc
codex.cx-campichu.body: Campichu is also a city of Tangut, and a very great and noble one. Indeed it is the capital and place of government of the whole province of Tangut.
codex.cx-campichu.name: Campichu
codex.cx-camul.body: Camul is a province which in former days was a kingdom. It contains numerous towns and villages, but the chief city bears the name of CAMUL. The province lies between the two deserts;
codex.cx-camul.name: Camul
codex.cx-caracoron.body: Caracoron is a city of some three miles in compass. [It is surrounded by a strong earthen rampart, for stone is scarce there.
codex.cx-caracoron.name: Caracoron
codex.cx-cascar.body: Cascar is a region lying between north-east and east, and constituted a kingdom in former days, but now it is subject to the Great Kaan. The people worship Mahommet. There are a good number of towns and villages, but the greatest and finest is Cascar itself.
codex.cx-cascar.name: Cascar
codex.cx-chamba.body: You must know that on leaving the port of Zayton you sail west-south-west for 1500 miles, and then you come to a country called CHAMBA, a very rich region, having a king of its own.
codex.cx-chamba.name: Chamba
codex.cx-chandu.body: And when you have ridden three days from the city last mentioned, between north-east and north, you come to a city called CHANDU, which was built by the Kaan now reigning.
codex.cx-chandu.name: Chandu
codex.cx-charchan.body: Charchan is a Province of Great Turkey, lying between north-east and east. The people worship Mahommet. There are numerous towns and villages, and the chief city of the kingdom bears its name, Charchan.
codex.cx-charchan.name: Charchan
codex.cx-chinangli.body: Chinangli is a city of Cathay as you go south, and it belongs to the Great Kaan; the people are Idolaters, and have paper-money. There runs through the city a great and wide river, on which a large traffic in silk goods and spices and other costly merchandize passes up and down.
codex.cx-chinangli.name: Chinangli
codex.cx-chinghianfu.body: Chinghianfu is a city of Manzi. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan, and have paper-money, and live by handicrafts and trade. They have plenty of silk, from which they make sundry kinds of stuffs of silk and gold. There are great and wealthy merchants in the place;
codex.cx-chinghianfu.name: Chinghianfu
codex.cx-chinginju.body: Leaving the city of Chinghianfu and travelling three days south-east through a constant succession of busy and thriving towns and villages, you arrive at the great and noble city of CHINGINJU. The people are Idolaters, use paper-money, and are subject to the Great Kaan.
codex.cx-chinginju.name: Chinginju
codex.cx-cobinan.body: Cobinan is a large town. The people worship Mahommet. There is much Iron and Steel and _Ondanique_, and they make steel mirrors of great size and beauty. They also prepare both _Tutia_ (a thing very good for the eyes) and _Spodium_; and I will tell you the process.
codex.cx-cobinan.name: Cobinan
codex.cx-coiganju.body: Coiganju is, as I have told you already, a very large city standing at the entrance to Manzi. The people are Idolaters and burn their dead, and are subject to the Great Kaan. They have a vast amount of shipping, as I mentioned before in speaking of the River Caramoran.
codex.cx-coiganju.name: Coiganju
codex.cx-coilum.body: When you quit Maabar and go 500 miles towards the south-west you come to the kingdom of COILUM. The people are Idolaters, but there are also some Christians and some Jews. The natives have a language of their own, and a King of their own, and are tributary to no one.
codex.cx-coilum.name: Coilum
codex.cx-cotan.body: Cotan is a province lying between north-east and east, and is eight days’ journey in length. The people are subject to the Great Kaan, and are all worshippers of Mahommet.
codex.cx-cotan.name: Cotan
codex.cx-desert-of-lop.name: Desert Of Lop
codex.cx-desert-voices.name: Desert Voices
codex.cx-dufar.body: Dufar is a great and noble and fine city, and lies 500 miles to the north-west of Esher. The people are Saracens, and have a Count for their chief, who is subject to the Soldan of Aden; for this city still belongs to the Province of Aden.
codex.cx-dufar.name: Dufar
codex.cx-egrigaia.body: Starting again from Erguiul you ride eastward for eight days, and then come to a province called EGRIGAIA, containing numerous cities and villages, and belonging to Tangut. The capital city is called CALACHAN.
codex.cx-egrigaia.name: Egrigaia
codex.cx-esher.body: Esher is a great city lying in a north-westerly direction from the last, and 400 miles distant from the Port of Aden. It has a king, who is subject to the Soldan of Aden. He has a number of towns and villages under him, and administers his territory well and justly. The people are Saracens.
codex.cx-esher.name: Esher
codex.cx-etzina.body: When you leave the city of Campichu you ride for twelve days, and then reach a city called ETZINA, which is towards the north on the verge of the Sandy Desert; it belongs to the Province of Tangut.
codex.cx-etzina.name: Etzina
codex.cx-fanfang.body: A street of the port given over to the merchants of India, Persia and the Arab lands, with their own houses of prayer standing within hearing of the sea-goddess's gongs.
codex.cx-fanfang.name: The Foreign Quarter
codex.cx-four-pillars.name: Four Pillars
codex.cx-fuju.body: Now this city of Fuju is the key of the kingdom which is called CHONKA, and which is one of the nine great divisions of Manzi. The city is a seat of great trade and great manufactures. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan.
codex.cx-fuju.name: Fuju
codex.cx-hexagrams.name: Hexagrams
codex.cx-hundred-shiploads.body: For every shipload of pepper that reaches Alexandria bound for Christendom, a hundred come in to Zayton. It is one of the two greatest havens in the world for commerce.
codex.cx-hundred-shiploads.name: A Hundred Shiploads
codex.cx-jade-rivers.name: Jade Rivers
codex.cx-kenjanfu.body: And when you leave the city of Cachanfu of which I have spoken, and travel eight days westward, you meet with cities and boroughs abounding in trade and industry, and quantities of beautiful trees, and gardens, and fine plains planted with mulberries, which are the trees on the leaves of which the s
codex.cx-kenjanfu.name: Kenjanfu
codex.cx-kerman.body: Kerman is a kingdom which is also properly in Persia, and formerly it had a hereditary prince. Since the Tartars conquered the country the rule is no longer hereditary, but the Tartar sends to administer whatever lord he pleases.
codex.cx-kerman.name: Kerman
codex.cx-keshimur.body: Keshimur also is a Province inhabited by a people who are Idolaters and have a language of their own. They have an astonishing acquaintance with the devilries of enchantment; insomuch that they make their idols to speak.
codex.cx-keshimur.name: Keshimur
codex.cx-kinsay.body: When you have left the city of Changan and have travelled for three days through a splendid country, passing a number of towns and villages, you arrive at the most noble city of KINSAY, a name which is as much as to say in our tongue “The City of Heaven,” as I told you before.
codex.cx-kinsay.name: Kinsay
codex.cx-linju.body: On leaving the city of Sinju-matu you travel for eight days towards the south, always coming to great and rich towns and villages flourishing with trade and manufactures. The people are all subjects of the Great Kaan, use paper-money, and burn their dead.
codex.cx-linju.name: Linju
codex.cx-lots.body: The cylinder is shaken until a single numbered slip falls out. The number is read against a book of verses. The verse does not answer the question asked; it names the thing the asker had not weighed.
codex.cx-lots.name: Reading the Slips
codex.cx-maabar.body: When you leave the Island of Seilan and sail westward about 60 miles, you come to the great province of MAABAR which is styled INDIA THE GREATER; it is best of all the Indies and is on the mainland. You must know that in this province there are five kings, who are own brothers.
codex.cx-maabar.name: Maabar
codex.cx-melibar.body: Melibar is a great kingdom lying towards the west. The people are Idolaters; they have a language of their own, and a king of their own, and pay tribute to nobody. In this country you see more of the North Star, for it shows two cubits above the water.
codex.cx-melibar.name: Melibar
codex.cx-mien.body: And when you have travelled those 15 days through such a difficult country as I have described, in which travellers have to carry provisions for the road because there are no inhabitants, then you arrive at the capital city of this Province of Mien, and it also is called AMIEN, and is a very great a
codex.cx-mien.name: Mien
codex.cx-monsoon.body: The wind of the Indian sea turns with the seasons. Ships out of Zayton for the Indies wait upon it, and a master who sails against it does not come back to say so.
codex.cx-monsoon.name: The Monsoon
codex.cx-nanghin.body: Nanghin is a very noble Province towards the west. The people are Idolaters (and so forth) and live by trade and manufactures. They have silk in great abundance, and they weave many fine tissues of silk and gold.
codex.cx-nanghin.name: Nanghin
codex.cx-ormus.body: The Plain of which we have spoken extends in a southerly direction for five days’ journey, and then you come to another descent some twenty miles in length, where the road is very bad and full of peril, for there are many robbers and bad characters about.
codex.cx-ormus.name: Ormus
codex.cx-paukin.body: When you leave Coiganju you ride south-east for a day along a causeway laid with fine stone, which you find at this entrance to Manzi. On either hand there is a great expanse of water, so that you cannot enter the province except along this causeway.
codex.cx-paukin.name: Paukin
codex.cx-pein.body: Pein is a province five days in length, lying between east and north-east. The people are worshippers of Mahommet, and subjects of the Great Kaan. There are a good number of towns and villages, but the most noble is PEIN, the capital of the kingdom.
codex.cx-pein.name: Pein
codex.cx-pentam.body: When you leave Locac and sail for 500 miles towards the south, you come to an island called PENTAM, a very wild place. All the wood that grows thereon consists of odoriferous trees. There is no more to say about it; so let us sail about sixty miles further between those two Islands.
codex.cx-pentam.name: Pentam
codex.cx-pepper-freight.body: Thirty in the hundred on small wares, forty on lignaloes and sandalwood and other bulky goods, and four and forty on pepper.
codex.cx-pepper-freight.name: Freight Rates at Zayton
codex.cx-road-23.name: Road 23
codex.cx-road-24.name: Road 24
codex.cx-road-25.name: Road 25
codex.cx-road-26.name: Road 26
codex.cx-road-27.name: Road 27
codex.cx-road-28.name: Road 28
codex.cx-road-29.name: Road 29
codex.cx-road-30.name: Road 30
codex.cx-saianfu.body: Saianfu is a very great and noble city, and it rules over twelve other large and rich cities, and is itself a seat of great trade and manufacture. The people are Idolaters (and so forth). They have much silk, from which they weave fine silken stuffs;
codex.cx-saianfu.name: Saianfu
codex.cx-samarcanda.body: Samarcan is a great and noble city towards the north-west, inhabited by both Christians and Saracens, who are subject to the Great Kaan’s nephew, CAIDOU by name; he is, however, at bitter enmity with the Kaan. I will tell you of a great marvel that happened at this city.
codex.cx-samarcanda.name: Samarcanda
codex.cx-sapurgan.body: On leaving the Castle, you ride over fine plains and beautiful valleys, and pretty hill-sides producing excellent grass pasture, and abundance of fruits, and all other products. Armies are glad to take up their quarters here on account of the plenty that exists.
codex.cx-sapurgan.name: Sapurgan
codex.cx-sea-goddess.body: A goddess of this coast to whom shipmasters go before sailing. Her temple keeps a cylinder of numbered slips; a slip is drawn and read against a book of verses.
codex.cx-sea-goddess.name: The Goddess of the Sea
codex.cx-semenat.body: Semenat is a great kingdom towards the west. The people are Idolaters, and have a king and a language of their own, and pay tribute to nobody. They are not corsairs, but live by trade and industry as honest people ought. It is a place of very great trade.
codex.cx-semenat.name: Semenat
codex.cx-siju.body: When you leave Piju you travel towards the south for two days, through beautiful districts abounding in everything, and in which you find quantities of all kinds of game. At the end of those two days you reach the city of SIJU, a great, rich, and noble city, flourishing with trade and manufactures.
codex.cx-siju.name: Siju
codex.cx-sindafu.body: When you have travelled those 20 days westward through the mountains, as I have told you, then you arrive at a plain belonging to a province called Sindafu, which still is on the confines of Manzi, and the capital city of which is (also) called SINDAFU.
codex.cx-sindafu.name: Sindafu
codex.cx-sinju.body: You must know that when you leave the city of Yanju, after going 15 miles south-east, you come to a city called SINJU, of no great size, but possessing a very great amount of shipping and trade. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan, and use paper-money.
codex.cx-sinju.name: Sinju
codex.cx-sinjumatu.body: On leaving Tadinfu you travel three days towards the south, always finding numbers of noble and populous towns and villages flourishing with trade and manufactures. There is also abundance of game in the country, and everything in profusion.
codex.cx-sinjumatu.name: Sinjumatu
codex.cx-suju.body: Suju is a very great and noble city. The people are Idolaters, subjects of the Great Kaan, and have paper-money. They possess silk in great quantities, from which they make gold brocade and other stuffs, and they live by their manufactures and trade.
codex.cx-suju.name: Suju
codex.cx-taican.body: After those twelve days’ journey you come to a fortified place called TAICAN, where there is a great corn market. It is a fine place, and the mountains that you see towards the south are all composed of salt.
codex.cx-taican.name: Taican
codex.cx-tana.body: Tana is a great kingdom lying towards the west, a kingdom great both in size and worth. The people are Idolaters, with a language of their own, and a king of their own, and tributary to nobody. No pepper grows there, nor other spices, but plenty of incense; not the white kind however, but brown.
codex.cx-tana.name: Tana
codex.cx-tangut-rites.name: Tangut Rites
codex.cx-tanpiju.body: When you leave Kinsay and travel a day’s journey to the south-east, through a plenteous region, passing a succession of dwellings and charming gardens, you reach the city of TANPIJU, a great, rich, and fine city, under Kinsay.
codex.cx-tanpiju.name: Tanpiju
codex.cx-tarot.name: Tarot
codex.cx-tauris.body: Tauris is a great and noble city, situated in a great province called YRAC, in which are many other towns and villages. But as Tauris is the most noble I will tell you about it.
codex.cx-tauris.name: Tauris
codex.cx-tenduc.body: Tenduc is a province which lies towards the east, and contains numerous towns and villages; among which is the chief city, also called TENDUC. The king of the province is of the lineage of Prester John, George by name, and he holds the land under the Great Kaan;
codex.cx-tenduc.name: Tenduc
codex.cx-tiju.body: When you leave Cayu, you ride another day to the south-east through a constant succession of villages and fields and fine farms until you come to TIJU, which is a city of no great size but abounding in everything. The people are Idolaters (and so forth).
codex.cx-tiju.name: Tiju
codex.cx-yarcan.body: Yarcan is a province five days’ journey in extent. The people follow the Law of Mahommet, but there are also Nestorian and Jacobite Christians. They are subject to the same Prince that I mentioned, the Great Kaan’s nephew. They have plenty of everything, [particularly of cotton.
codex.cx-yarcan.name: Yarcan
codex.cx-yasdi.body: Yasdi also is properly in Persia; it is a good and noble city, and has a great amount of trade. They weave there quantities of a certain silk tissue known as _Yasdi_, which merchants carry into many quarters to dispose of. The people are worshippers of Mahommet.
codex.cx-yasdi.name: Yasdi
codex.cx-zayton-tithe.body: Ten in the hundred on all merchandise landed at Zayton, including precious stones and pearls — the Great Kaan takes the tamghā on everything. With the ship's freight added, a merchant pays out half his cargo's worth before he has sold a grain of it.
codex.cx-zayton-tithe.name: The Kaan's Tamghā
div.astrodice.name: Astrodice
div.astrodice.result.00: Great fortune: the dice name a morning departure before the heat rises.
div.astrodice.result.01: The dice name a three-day wait: the next caravan is better company.
div.astrodice.result.02: The dice name the north gate; the south road is crowded with tax clerks.
div.astrodice.result.03: The dice name a short leg only; do not press beyond the next well.
div.astrodice.result.04: The dice name bargaining at dusk, when the stalls lower their first prices.
div.astrodice.result.05: The dice name a translator before any contract is sealed.
div.astrodice.result.06: The dice name inland forage; the coast wind turns against shipping.
div.astrodice.result.07: The dice name lodging near the mosque courtyard, not the riverbank.
div.astrodice.result.08: The dice name paying the toll in full and asking no favours.
div.astrodice.result.09: The dice name sending a scout ahead to the next caravanserai.
div.astrodice.result.10: The dice name postponing the mountain pass until after the new moon.
div.astrodice.result.11: The dice name buying water-skins here; they will be dearer ahead.
div.astrodice.result.12: The dice name travelling with the spice merchants, not alone.
div.astrodice.result.13: The dice name avoiding night watches on the open steppe.
div.astrodice.result.14: The dice name changing horses at the next post, not this one.
div.astrodice.result.15: Ill omen: the dice name postponing the mountain pass until after the new moon.
div.astrodice.result.16: The dice name resting one day for a lame camel rather than forcing the march.
div.astrodice.result.17: The dice name asking the astrologer of this court which month the road opens.
div.astrodice.result.18: The dice name keeping silver divided among three purses.
div.astrodice.result.19: The dice name taking the longer river road; the short cut floods.
div.astrodice.result.20: The dice name waiting for the Friday market before you sell.
div.astrodice.result.21: The dice name speaking little of your destination in this inn.
div.astrodice.result.22: The dice name hiring a local watch for the warehouse night.
div.astrodice.result.23: The dice name not crossing the ferry until the boatmen sober after noon.
div.astrodice.result.24: The dice name reading the wind for two dawns before you sail.
div.astrodice.result.25: The dice name seeking the Armenian quarter for news of the inland road.
div.astrodice.result.26: The dice name not trusting the first guide who greets you at the gate.
div.astrodice.result.27: The dice name marking the wells on your tablet before you leave.
div.astrodice.result.28: The dice name offering a small gift at the shrine before you bargain.
div.astrodice.result.29: The dice name choosing the road that still has shade at noon.
div.bazi-relationship.name: Pillars Compatibility
div.bazi.apprentice: The astrologer studies your birth date with narrowed eyes, drawing a chart of eight characters in black ink. 'Your wood is strong but your fire is weak,' she says. 'This is not a judgment. It is a compass. The roads that suit a fire person will burn you out. The roads that suit a wood person will let you grow. I will teach you to read your own chart — but first you must accept that you cannot walk every road.'
div.bazi.desc: The Four Pillars of Destiny examine the hour, day, month, and year of your birth against the elemental cycles of wood, fire, earth, metal, and water. The chart reveals what kind of traveller you are — which regions suit your nature, which companions strengthen you, and which years bring opportunity. Cost: 400 coins. Horizon: three years.
div.bazi.name: Four Pillars
div.bazi.result.00: [route] Your day-master is firm. Take the steady official road; do not gamble on shortcuts.
div.bazi.result.01: [route] The yearly water is strong; river crossings have a wider window of safe passage.
div.bazi.result.02: [route] Earth energy is full. Stay on the long overland road; avoid switching boats too often.
div.bazi.result.03: [route] Metal energy is strong. Bargain firmly, but do not offend the gate clerks.
div.bazi.result.04: [route] Wood energy rises. Set out early, and ask often about new routes.
div.bazi.result.05: [route] Fire energy is parched. Rest at midday in summer; do not travel under the noon sun.
div.bazi.result.06: [route] The day-pillar advises: hiring an interpreter matters more than meeting a merchant.
div.bazi.result.07: [route] The year-pillar is stable. Longer contracts are worth signing.
div.bazi.result.08: [route] The month-command is weak. Shorten each leg of the journey.
div.bazi.result.09: [route] The hour-pillar stirs. At the fork, cast the coins again before deciding.
div.bazi.result.10: [route] Water is missing from the chart. Choose roads that follow the river.
div.bazi.result.11: [route] Fire is missing from the chart. Camp near settlements at night.
div.bazi.result.12: [route] Competing elements are many. Travel with few companions and clear rules.
div.bazi.result.13: [route] Expressive stars shine. Good for gathering news of goods and market prices.
div.bazi.result.14: [route] Wealth stars are visible. Linger in the market, but not at the posting station.
div.bazi.result.15: [route] Authority stars weigh heavily. Prepare your documents in full before the checkpoint.
div.bazi.result.16: [route] A seal star protects. Lodge in a city that has a temple or monastery.
div.bazi.result.17: [route] A luck cycle change approaches. Delay any major change of route.
div.bazi.result.18: [route] This chart says: travel east to study, west to trade.
div.bazi.result.19: [route] Your birth season hints: in autumn, depart early; in spring, depart steady.
div.bazi.result.20: [route] The day-branch clashes. Do not share a room or discuss strategy with someone of the same sign.
div.bazi.result.21: [route] Heavenly stems combine. Hire camels together with a partner; do not take it all on your own.
div.bazi.result.22: [route] Earthly branches open. Go slow on mountain paths; speed on the plain.
div.bazi.result.23: [route] Void descends on the road. Do not trust unfounded rumours of a shortcut.
div.bazi.result.24: [route] Salary and blade are both clear. Travel with a familiar merchant group.
div.bazi.result.25: [route] Weather needs water. Take the sea leg before the dry stretch.
div.bazi.result.26: [route] Weather needs fire. Choose valley roads with long hours of sunlight.
div.bazi.result.27: [route] This chart says: for three years, let trade support your learning, not the other way.
div.bazi.result.28: [route] The post-horse star moves. In a year of frequent shifts, lighten your cargo.
div.bazi.result.29: [route] A canopy star descends. Visit a local teacher before settling on a long route.

div.geomancy.name: Geomancy
div.geomancy.result.00: The figure opens the road if you keep to the caravan hours.
div.geomancy.result.01: Great fortune: the figure opens a side gate; ask the porter for the merchants' entrance.
div.geomancy.result.02: The figure opens trade in salt and hides; leave silks for another city.
div.geomancy.result.03: The figure opens a morning audience; do not wait until the heat.
div.geomancy.result.04: The figure opens the desert road only with two spare water-skins.
div.geomancy.result.05: The figure opens learning the local prayer times before you bargain.
div.geomancy.result.06: The figure opens hiring a watchman for your packs at the inn.
div.geomancy.result.07: The figure opens a short stay; leave before the weekly tax count.
div.geomancy.result.08: The figure opens asking the qadi's clerk which roads are under ban.
div.geomancy.result.09: The figure opens sharing a fire with the next company, not camping alone.
div.geomancy.result.10: The figure holds you one day: mend harness before you go.
div.geomancy.result.11: The figure holds counsel: write the distances between wells tonight.
div.geomancy.result.12: The figure holds: do not sell until you have heard three prices.
div.geomancy.result.13: The figure holds: wait for the dust storm to pass the ridge.
div.geomancy.result.14: The figure holds: keep your letters sealed until the next city.
div.geomancy.result.15: Great ill omen: the figure stops the night march; daylight only on this band.
div.geomancy.result.16: The figure stops a bargain with a man who will not name his city.
div.geomancy.result.17: The figure stops crossing the river at this ford; go upstream.
div.geomancy.result.18: The figure stops trusting maps drawn in another season.
div.geomancy.result.19: The figure stops paying guides who demand half in advance.
div.geomancy.result.20: The figure stops entering the warehouse quarter after dark.
div.geomancy.result.21: The figure stops arguing tolls; pay and keep moving.
div.geomancy.result.22: The figure stops dividing your company on this plain.
div.geomancy.result.23: The figure stops opening wine before the next shrine.
div.geomancy.result.24: The figure stops chasing rumour of a shorter road east.
div.geomancy.result.25: The figure warns: the next well may be guarded; approach with gifts.
div.geomancy.result.26: The figure warns: leave heavy cargo and send a light scout first.
div.geomancy.result.27: The figure warns: do not sleep in the ruined caravanserai.
div.geomancy.result.28: The figure warns: change your planned day of departure by one.
div.geomancy.result.29: The figure warns: ask again after you have seen the sky clear.
div.iching.apprentice: The old scholar unrolls a strip of yellow silk covered with broken and unbroken lines. 'These are not fortunes,' he says. 'They are maps. Each hexagram is a landscape — mountains, rivers, thunder, wind. You do not ask if you will succeed. You ask: which road through this landscape is mine?' He places three coins in your open palm. 'Cast them. We will read what the earth writes.'
div.iching.desc: The Book of Changes reveals the shape of the road ahead. Ask not whether fortune favours you, but which direction aligns with the moment. Cast three coins six times to form a hexagram; each line speaks of movement or stillness. The reading shows which routes open and which close. Cost: 200 coins. Horizon: one season.
div.iching.hex.0.advice: Force favours action with clear purpose. Choose the main road and set out at dawn; do not wait for a companion who hesitates.
div.iching.hex.1.advice: The Field receives what comes. Follow a route that others have travelled and marked; carry less than you think you need.
div.iching.hex.10.advice: The third of three passes opens. The high road is open, the low road is open, the grass is firm. Move without delay.
div.iching.hex.11.advice: Heaven presses earth and doors close. Do not set out against the season; wait three days and try the next station.
div.iching.hex.12.advice: You will find company on this road, even where you expect none. Share your fire with a stranger tonight.
div.iching.hex.13.advice: The holdings are full and the road is clear. Trade what you carry before you reach the market; the price is good at the next halt.
div.iching.hex.14.advice: The mountain bows beneath heaven. Cross the high ground by the lower pass, and let the guides name the way.
div.iching.hex.15.advice: Thunder rises out of earth, and readiness is its own reward. Rise early and prepare for news at the second post.
div.iching.hex.16.advice: The cart follows the ruts that came before. Do not strike a new trail when the old road still holds water.
div.iching.hex.17.advice: The vessel is cracked but still carries water. Mend what you carry before setting out, even if it costs you a day.
div.iching.hex.18.advice: The marsh comes to the shore — approach the next city in company, not alone, for the guards watch the lone traveller harder.
div.iching.hex.19.advice: Look down from the tower before you descend to the gate. Watch the traffic for one watch before choosing your road.
div.iching.hex.2.advice: A beginning is tangled and heavy. Leave by the side gate and walk the smaller road; the main way is thick with carts this season.
div.iching.hex.20.advice: Bite through what resists you. Pay the gate toll without argument and keep your purse hidden until the city square.
div.iching.hex.21.advice: The ornament hides what lies beneath. Do not judge the road by the welcome; ask the market porters where the dust runs deep.
div.iching.hex.22.advice: The mountain crumbles. Travel light and do not trust the old bridge; take the ford instead, even if it costs a wet boot.
div.iching.hex.23.advice: What returns after winter is stronger than what stayed. A road closed last season may open again; ask at the station again.
div.iching.hex.24.advice: No false thread holds this weave. Trust the directions you received; do not listen to shortcuts told at the wine stall.
div.iching.hex.25.advice: The mountain holds great stores. Stock your bags here, for the next three stations keep poor markets.
div.iching.hex.26.advice: Nourish your company and your body. Spend a full day resting before the mountain crossing; thin travellers are stopped at the pass.
div.iching.hex.27.advice: The beam is too heavy for the house. Do not carry a full cargo on the desert road; split your goods or sell half.
div.iching.hex.28.advice: Water over water — the ford is deeper than it looks. Wait for a local boatman; do not cross alone.
div.iching.hex.29.advice: Fire holds to what feeds it. Attach yourself to a caravan even if it costs you coin; a lone flame draws bandits.
div.iching.hex.3.advice: A spring under a mountain runs blind. Ask the herders, not the merchants, which path the goats take to water.
div.iching.hex.30.advice: Influence draws like to like. Speak gently at the next toll house, and the guard may know which innkeepers trade in maps.
div.iching.hex.31.advice: Thunder and wind endure together. Choose the road that keeps the river in sight; do not turn inland for a rumour.
div.iching.hex.32.advice: The wise man retreats to higher ground before the flood. Skip the next river town and climb to the hill station.
div.iching.hex.33.advice: Great strength moves the cart through mud. Take the lowland marsh road while the dry season holds; do not delay.
div.iching.hex.34.advice: The sun advances over the plain — ride or walk while the light is full. Do not begin a stage in the last hour of day.
div.iching.hex.35.advice: Light is wounded but not extinguished. Travel the coast road at night under the moon; avoid midday heat on this stage.
div.iching.hex.36.advice: The household feeds itself before the road. Settle your accounts at this city before you take a single step out.
div.iching.hex.37.advice: Two faces look opposite ways. Your map and your guide disagree; stand still half a day and ask a third voice.
div.iching.hex.38.advice: The mountain blocks the water. Turn back at the landslide, even if you lose a day; the goat track is not a road.
div.iching.hex.39.advice: Thunder loosens the rain at last. The blocked road will open after the storm; wait in the caravanserai and bargain for provisions.
div.iching.hex.4.advice: Wait one more day. The ford is swollen with meltwater; a boat will come with the morning barge.
div.iching.hex.40.advice: Decrease opens the jar for pouring. Give a little of your cargo as gifts at the pass, and the guards will wave you through.
div.iching.hex.41.advice: Increase lifts the vessel higher. Accept a travelling companion who knows the language of the next province.
div.iching.hex.42.advice: Resolution parts the flooding waters. Choose now: the mountain road or the sea lane; drifting between them loses both.
div.iching.hex.43.advice: Encounter favours the first meeting. Approach the next city when the gate opens, not after the midday market thins, for the first buyer learns most.
div.iching.hex.44.advice: The marsh gathers streams into one pool. Gather news from three sources before you commit to a route across the steppe.
div.iching.hex.45.advice: The tree climbs the southern slope. Take the ascending ridge road, not the valley path; the melt has swollen the low streams.
div.iching.hex.46.advice: Confinement is a wall with a gate you have not yet tried. The main road is closed; ask the temple keeper about the pilgrim way.
div.iching.hex.47.advice: The well water is clear but the rope is short. Your coin is enough for the journey but not enough for haste; travel slowly.
div.iching.hex.48.advice: The hide is stripped — revolution remakes the old shape. Do not travel by the trade route this season; try the pilgrim road.
div.iching.hex.49.advice: The cauldron holds what feeds the village. Cook your own food on the road, even when the inn promises a hot meal.
div.iching.hex.5.advice: A dispute at the gate wastes daylight. Pay the claimed toll without raising your voice; the road beyond is worth more than the copper.
div.iching.hex.50.advice: A hundred li away, thunder rolls. Word will reach the next city before you do; arrive quietly and listen before you speak.
div.iching.hex.51.advice: Two mountains — stillness doubled at the pass. Do not cross the col today; the wind is turning and the cloud is low.
div.iching.hex.52.advice: The wild goose walks into the marsh one step at a time. Take the journey by short stages, resting at every well.
div.iching.hex.53.advice: The maiden joins the new house, and all alters. Your known maps end here; hire a local guide, not a merchant from the last city.
div.iching.hex.54.advice: Thunder and lightning fill the sky with abundance. The road buzzes with news and caravans; join a large company and keep your own pace.
div.iching.hex.55.advice: The traveller's fire must be small and quick. Sleep in a different inn each night; do not let any town grow accustomed to your face.
div.iching.hex.56.advice: The wind bends the reeds without breaking them. Adapt your route when the road is blocked; do not force a passage through closed country.
div.iching.hex.57.advice: The marsh mirrors the sky, and joy comes to those who rest. Pause a full day at the lake town and let the mules drink deep.
div.iching.hex.58.advice: The waters scatter and must gather again. Half your company will leave for another road today; choose which ones to follow yourself.
div.iching.hex.59.advice: The bamboo joint limits what passes through. Carry only what you can lift alone past the narrow gate.
div.iching.hex.6.advice: The host must know the ground. Before you travel a new road, send word ahead through a caravanserai runner.
div.iching.hex.60.advice: Inner truth moves even across still water. Follow the route your heart settled on at dawn, even if three merchants warn you away.
div.iching.hex.61.advice: A small excess tips the scale. Take slightly more water than your skin can hold and slightly less coin than you planned to carry.
div.iching.hex.62.advice: You have already crossed the greater part and only the last ford remains. Do not relax at the final station.
div.iching.hex.63.advice: You are not yet across — the far bank is in sight but the boatman is on the other side. Light a fire on the shore and wait for morning.
div.iching.hex.7.advice: Grouping holds the men around a single well. Choose a road where caravans gather; a bare road this month means bandit sign.
div.iching.hex.8.advice: Small restraint gathers strength for the climb. Do not leave today; one more night in this city will put the road in your favour.
div.iching.hex.9.advice: Tread carefully where the path is narrow. The mountain track holds ice in the shadow; let the mule test every step.
div.iching.name: I Ching
div.iching.result.00: This hexagram favours a slow overland march. Ask at the posting station before you plan the route.
div.iching.result.01: The moving lines are many. Reroute to the nearest walled town and rest three days.
div.iching.result.02: The timing and position are against a river crossing. Wait until the wind settles before you wade.
div.iching.result.03: The western road has dense caravans and easy news. Ask about prices but do not buy in haste.
div.iching.result.04: The northern road has strict checkpoints. Prepare your papers and an interpreter first.
div.iching.result.05: The sea monsoon is not yet stable. Take short coast-hugging stages instead.
div.iching.result.06: Travel in company on this leg. If you go alone, ask less often and pause more.
div.iching.result.07: Before the pass, offer a small gift and then ask the hours of passage.
div.iching.result.08: Pack rations for twice the expected days; the dry stretch has no resupply.
div.iching.result.09: Stay briefly in this city. Do not linger haggling — you may lose your weather window.
div.iching.result.10: The post road forks. Take the branch that has a well.
div.iching.result.11: Night travel is not favoured. Set out at first light.
div.iching.result.12: This hexagram advises: learn the tax rules before entering the market.
div.iching.result.13: Among your company is one who knows the road. Ask them to walk ahead.
div.iching.result.14: Lighten the camel train. Do not carry a full load on the mountain path.
div.iching.result.15: The ferry crossing is crowded. Circle upstream to the shallow ford.
div.iching.result.16: On this leg, secure lodging before you open trade.
div.iching.result.17: The wind is turning. Sea-going vessels should wait two more days.
div.iching.result.18: Prices at the border market are inflated. Compare three stalls before you decide.
div.iching.result.19: The gate clerks rotate soon. Pass through while the old rules still stand.
div.iching.result.20: Travel the desert stretch by night and rest by day.
div.iching.result.21: This hexagram favours hiring a guide. Do not trust an old map alone.
div.iching.result.22: The river ice is about to melt. Find a wooden bridge instead of fording.
div.iching.result.23: The city gate closes at dusk. Enter early.
div.iching.result.24: The trade road has reports of robbery. Switch to the official highway.
div.iching.result.25: Carry salt and tea as gifts on this leg; they open doors faster than words.
div.iching.result.26: Post-horses are scarce. Alternate walking and riding stretches.
div.iching.result.27: The rains are coming. Cross the valley before the mud sets in.
div.iching.result.28: This hexagram says: ask about the water source before you choose a campsite.
div.iching.result.29: The destination city has a festival. Enter early to secure an inn.
div.jiaobei.name: Jiaobei
div.jiaobei.result.00: Great fortune: the cups grant leave to ask the road of the next town before you choose.
div.jiaobei.result.01: The cups grant leave to hire a guide for the mountain pass.
div.jiaobei.result.02: The cups grant leave to wait one tide before boarding.
div.jiaobei.result.03: The cups grant leave to buy grain here; the next market will be dearer.
div.jiaobei.result.04: The cups grant leave to speak first at the gate, and plainly.
div.jiaobei.result.05: The cups grant leave to take the inland road; the shore road is watched.
div.jiaobei.result.06: The cups grant leave to join the caravan that leaves at dawn.
div.jiaobei.result.07: The cups grant leave to lodge within walls tonight.
div.jiaobei.result.08: The cups grant leave to change silver before the frontier.
div.jiaobei.result.09: The cups grant leave to ask three prices before you buy.
div.jiaobei.result.10: Great ill omen: the cups refuse the crossing today; seek another ford tomorrow.
div.jiaobei.result.11: The cups refuse night travel; wait for the second watch of morning.
div.jiaobei.result.12: The cups refuse a bargain struck in haste at this stall.
div.jiaobei.result.13: The cups refuse the short desert cut; keep to the wells.
div.jiaobei.result.14: The cups refuse to open a sealed letter on the road.
div.jiaobei.result.15: The cups refuse sailing under this wind; another day.
div.jiaobei.result.16: The cups refuse hiring the loudest guide in the square.
div.jiaobei.result.17: The cups refuse camping without a wall in sight.
div.jiaobei.result.18: The cups refuse paying the first toll named to you.
div.jiaobei.result.19: The cups refuse parting from the company you already have.
div.jiaobei.result.20: The cups laugh: ask again after you have counted your water-skins.
div.jiaobei.result.21: The cups laugh: ask again when the dust settles and you can see the posts.
div.jiaobei.result.22: The cups laugh: ask again once you have spoken to a local scribe.
div.jiaobei.result.23: The cups laugh: ask again after noon prayer when the bazaar thins.
div.jiaobei.result.24: The cups laugh: ask again with a clearer question of one road only.
div.jiaobei.result.25: The cups laugh: ask again after you sleep one night in this city.
div.jiaobei.result.26: The cups laugh: ask again when your companion is sober.
div.jiaobei.result.27: The cups laugh: ask again beside the temple threshold, not in the street.
div.jiaobei.result.28: The cups laugh: ask again after you have named the city you mean.
div.jiaobei.result.29: The cups laugh: ask again; this cast has nothing yet to say.

div.liuyao.name: Six Lines
div.lot.apprentice: The temple keeper shakes the bamboo cylinder until a single numbered stick clatters onto the stone floor. He picks it up, squints at the number, and turns to a cabinet of a hundred drawers. 'Each lot is a verse,' he says, selecting a slip of paper. 'Each verse is a warning or a permission. The gods do not prophesy — they advise. Learn to hear the difference, and you will never be lost.'
div.lot.desc: Temple lots give a direct answer to a single question — yes or no, with a warning. Shake the bamboo cylinder until one numbered stick falls. The keeper reads the corresponding verse from the book. Best for immediate decisions: Should I take this road today? Is this merchant honest? Cost: 50 coins. Horizon: one day.
div.lot.name: Temple Lots
div.lot.result.00: The lot says: advance along the planned posting stations; do not change the route at the last moment.
div.lot.result.01: The lot says: advance along the planned posting stations; do not change the route at the last moment.
div.lot.result.02: The lot warns: do not board a boat today. Wait for tomorrow's tide.
div.lot.result.03: The lot says: compare the same goods at three stalls before you buy.
div.lot.result.04: The lot says: join a caravan; do not walk the solitary stretch alone.
div.lot.result.05: The lot says: halt at this fork and return to the city for more provisions.
div.lot.result.06: The lot says: leave at dawn to avoid the checkpoint queues.
div.lot.result.07: The lot says: do not camp in the wild tonight; find a walled posting inn.
div.lot.result.08: The lot says: courtesy before questions at the pass shortens the delay.
div.lot.result.09: The lot says: hide your best goods in the market; do not display them.
div.lot.result.10: The lot says: where the tongue is strange, hire an interpreter before you negotiate.
div.lot.result.11: The lot says: two roads run equal; choose the one with wells.
div.lot.result.12: The lot says: wait one full tidal cycle before putting to sea.
div.lot.result.13: The lot says: lighten the load on the mountain road; split the cargo into two trips.
div.lot.result.14: The lot says: if anyone in your party is ill, treat them inside the city before you leave.
div.lot.result.15: The lot says: take the detour. The official road is longer but has fewer robbers.
div.lot.result.16: The lot says: learn the port tax rate before you enter the city.
div.lot.result.17: The lot says: keep your word. Do not delay a promised delivery date again.
div.lot.result.18: The lot says: curb your desire. Buy only what you need of this city's wares.
div.lot.result.19: The lot says: near the sea, visit the shrine to the sea-goddess before you sail.
div.lot.result.20: The lot says: when reports contradict, stop for one day before you decide.
div.lot.result.21: The lot says: travel north. The northern road has steadier resupply.
div.lot.result.22: The lot says: travel south. The monsoon is turning; consider the sea route.
div.lot.result.23: The lot says: travel west. Camel hire is cheap now; arrange your transport.
div.lot.result.24: The lot says: travel east. Documents are easy to obtain; checkpoints are lenient.
div.lot.result.25: The lot says: a short stop. Spend one night only; do not grow fond of the market.
div.lot.result.26: The lot says: a long stay. Learn the local tongue for a season before you move on.
div.lot.result.27: The lot says: a small gift for directions beats an empty word.
div.lot.result.28: The lot says: record the road conditions in your codex for the return journey.
div.lot.result.29: The lot says: ask one question per lot. Do not draw twice on the same day.

div.runes.name: Runes
div.runes.result.00: Great fortune: the rune names company — join the next wagon before the steppe widens.
div.runes.result.01: The rune names a river crossing at dawn, when the ice is still firm.
div.runes.result.02: The rune names speaking the northern tongue at the next post.
div.runes.result.03: The rune names a gift of salt to the first elder who greets you.
div.runes.result.04: The rune names marking the stars for three nights before you turn.
div.runes.result.05: The rune names keeping your sword visible but sheathed in this town.
div.runes.result.06: The rune names buying felt and not silk on this market day.
div.runes.result.07: The rune names a detour to the wooden church for news of the road.
div.runes.result.08: The rune names waiting out the blizzard in the stockaded yard.
div.runes.result.09: The rune names hiring a local boy who knows the wolf tracks.
div.runes.result.10: The rune names delay: one day for the ferry ropes to be mended.
div.runes.result.11: The rune names delay until the tribute train has passed.
div.runes.result.12: The rune names delay: dry your boots before the next marsh.
div.runes.result.13: Ill omen: the rune names danger on the reed bank; keep to the raised track.
div.runes.result.14: The rune names danger in the abandoned tower; do not shelter there.
div.runes.result.15: The rune names danger if you travel without a bell on the lead horse.
div.runes.result.16: The rune names an ally among the fur traders of this quay.
div.runes.result.17: The rune names an ally if you share bread at the gate-fire.
div.runes.result.18: The rune names travel light across the frozen lake; leave the cart.
div.runes.result.19: The rune names travel with the amber merchants bound west.
div.runes.result.20: The rune names travel only while the sun clears the pine line.
div.runes.result.21: The rune names holding your question until you reach the next idol-post.
div.runes.result.22: The rune names holding silver back from the first inn's reckoning.
div.runes.result.23: The rune names holding the southern fork; the northern is flooded.
div.runes.result.24: The rune names asking the Varangian guard which bridge still stands.
div.runes.result.25: The rune names writing the tribal passwords you are given tonight.
div.runes.result.26: The rune names not racing the horse that limps into the yard.
div.runes.result.27: The rune names counting your arrows before you leave the stockade.
div.runes.result.28: The rune names paying the ferryman what he asks; argue later ashore.
div.runes.result.29: The rune names turning back one station if the sky turns iron-grey.

div.tarot.name: Tarot
div.tarot.result.00: [route] The spread points to a steady road. Take the exit with clear resupply.
div.tarot.result.01: [route] A blocking card warns: the shortcut costs more than the official road.
div.tarot.result.02: [route] The resource card sits on the left. Westbound caravans can lend you strength.
div.tarot.result.03: [route] The resource card sits on the right. Eastbound posting stations are more reliable.
div.tarot.result.04: [route] The timeline shows past delays. Shorten today's stage.
div.tarot.result.05: [route] The present card demands: settle your interpreter before you discuss the route.
div.tarot.result.06: [route] The future card opens: within three days, the sea route becomes favourable.
div.tarot.result.07: [route] Door A brings high profit at the cost of time — choose it when your cargo is urgent.
div.tarot.result.08: [route] Door B costs coin but spares time — avoid it when your purse is lean.
div.tarot.result.09: [route] The principle card: let safety outweigh profit on this leg.
div.tarot.result.10: [route] A reversed blockage: do not sign a long hire contract today.
div.tarot.result.11: [route] A reversed excess: do not fill your cargo hold all at once.
div.tarot.result.12: [route] Upright passage: answer the checkpoint questions truthfully.
div.tarot.result.13: [route] A shadow card: do not trust a guide with no known origin.
div.tarot.result.14: [route] The environment card: this city is full of rumour; cross-check every report.
div.tarot.result.15: [route] The self card: the rhythm of the overland road suits you better.
div.tarot.result.16: [route] The outcome card: test the short road before you commit to the long one.
div.tarot.result.17: [route] The challenge card: the river crossing is this leg's key risk.
div.tarot.result.18: [route] The hope card: you can learn a new divination method at the next city.
div.tarot.result.19: [route] The fear card: do not abandon a known road because of a rumour.
div.tarot.result.20: [route] The career spread reads: first secure your position, then seek opportunity.
div.tarot.result.21: [route] The coin-flow points: your costs are in tariffs, not in transport hire.
div.tarot.result.22: [route] The relationship mirror: hear your companions' opinions, but the choice stays yours.
div.tarot.result.23: [route] One-card calibration: the watchword is hold fast, not charge ahead.
div.tarot.result.24: [route] One-card calibration: the watchword is ask first, not buy first.
div.tarot.result.25: [route] The three-card counsel: check the water level before you reroute.
div.tarot.result.26: [route] The Celtic-cross outcome: the long line still points to your original destination.
div.tarot.result.27: [route] Card combination: water dominates; choose roads near rivers and lakes.
div.tarot.result.28: [route] Card combination: fire dominates; avoid marching under the midday sun.
div.tarot.result.29: [route] Card combination: earth dominates; the dry road can carry heavy cargo.

end.cartographer.epilogue: {years} years and {cities} cities, and what you have to show is paper. The road from {longestRoute} is drawn to the day's march, with the water marked and the passes named. Others will use it and not know you. That is what a chart is for, and you knew it when you began.
end.cartographer.name: The Chart-Maker
end.diviner.epilogue: {cities} cities in {years} years, and in each of them you asked the same question in a different language. The stalks, the sticks, the cards and the stars do not agree, and you came to think that the disagreement is the answer. You keep {faith}, and you keep the others' methods too, which the learned of every city told you was impossible.
end.diviner.name: Reader of the Signs
end.lay_down.epilogue: You set out from {start} and you are stopping at {lastCity}: {cities} cities, {years} years, {faith} still, and {richestTrade} the best bargain you ever struck. The book ends because you have closed it, not because the road did. There is more of it. There was always going to be more of it.
end.lay_down.name: Laying Down the Pen
end.markets.epilogue: {years} years, {cities} cities, and a ledger that balances. You learned the thing the guidebooks cannot teach: that the same bale is two different goods in two places, and the distance between them is the whole of the profit. {richestTrade} was the making of you. You could name the day you understood it, and you never told anyone.
end.markets.name: Master of a Hundred Markets
end.no_return.epilogue: You crossed {cities} cities in {years} years and never came back to {start}. Some say you were last seen at {lastCity}; some say you died on the road. Both are true: a traveller's home is being spoken of, again and again.
end.no_return.name: The One Who Did Not Return
end.returned.epilogue: You came home to {start} after {years} years and {cities} cities, and found that the hardest part was the telling. Men who had never left the parish argued with you about the width of rivers. Of everything you carried back, it was {richestTrade} that made your fortune, and no one asked about it twice. The rest they did not believe, and you wrote it down anyway.
end.returned.name: The One Who Came Back
end.stayed.epilogue: You went out for a season and remained {years} years. {cities} cities are behind you and you are still at {lastCity}, which you no longer call by the name you learned it under. You keep {faith} as you always did, in a place that has its own arrangements about such things and does not press you. Venice is a word you can still spell.
end.stayed.name: The One Who Stayed
end.witness.epilogue: {cities} cities in {years} years, and the road from {longestRoute} the longest of them. You did not go as an envoy, and you did not go to trade; you went to see, and you saw. What you can report is small beside what there was: the tide of a river at a particular hour, the price of salt in a town with no name in any book. It is what a witness has.
end.witness.name: Witness of the World
ending.returned-to-venice.body: After {years} years on the road, you have returned to the city where you began. The Piazza San Marco is smaller than you remembered. The merchants who once seemed rich are now modest traders with modest horizons. Your cargo — {goods} — makes you the wealthiest man in Venice, but wealth no longer interests you. In the evenings, you stand on the Rialto and watch the ships you will never board, their holds full of pepper you no longer need to buy, bound for ports you have already seen. The Doge invites you to dinner; you tell the story of the {cities} cities you have passed through, and no one believes half of it. {faith} has taught you that the journey was the destination. The book you write will be called a fantasy. You will let them believe that.
ending.returned-to-venice.name: The Return
ending.stayed-in-the-east.body: You never went back. Somewhere on the {longestRoute} — the longest road you ever rode — you realised that the traveller you had become no longer belonged in the place that made you. You settled in {cities}, a city of {faith} prayers and merchants who speak {languages} languages. You took a local name. You married. Your children speak a tongue you learned as an adult. At night, when the traders arrive from the west, you listen to news of your birthplace the way you once listened to tales of Cathay — as a story about a country you have visited but no longer live in. In your old age, a young traveller arrives from Venice, full of questions. You answer none of them. Instead, you pour him tea and tell him about the road ahead.
ending.stayed-in-the-east.name: The East
ending.template: After {years} years of travel, you have seen {cities} cities. You crossed {deserts} deserts and sailed {seas} seas. The {longestRoute} taught you the most. {faith} sustained you when nothing else would. This is the story of how you became {final_title} — a name the road gave you, and the road will remember.
ending.witness-of-the-world.body: You have seen {cities} cities, crossed {deserts} deserts, and sailed {seas} seas. Your maps are the most accurate in the world, though only you can read them. Your journals fill a chest — prices, routes, customs, warnings, drawings of plants no physician has described, star-charts no astrologer has drawn. You are not the richest man in the world, nor the most powerful, but you are its greatest witness. When the scholars of {faith} come to interview you in your last years, you dictate for hours, days, weeks, until your voice gives out. They write it all down. The book they produce will be read for a hundred years, and every traveller who follows will follow your footsteps — whether they know your name or not. This is the only immortality that means anything: the road remembers.
ending.witness-of-the-world.name: The Witness
ev.accon.entry.body: Acre upon the Syrian shore — a great haven of the Franks on this coast. Pilgrims and Maghribī merchants come down from Damascus to seek passage here; the tithe is taken at the mole, a qīrāt in every dīnār of goods. Venetian and Genoese galleys unload woolens and take on spicery for the return. Between Acre and Jerusalem lie three days; the plain about the walls has no gardens, and fruit is brought in from the hill farms. You must know that Latin, Greek, and Arabic tongues are all heard upon these quays, and that the Templars' tower watches the roadstead.
ev.accon.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.accon.entry.title: Arriving at Accon
ev.aden.a.body: You stand upon the quay where the great ships of India discharge their cargoes into lighter craft. Men say the pepper and spicery must pass seven days by sea to a lesser haven, then thirty days by camel to the river of Alexandria, whence it descends to that city. No road of equal convenience serves the merchants of Egypt. The bales are weighed, marked, and stacked in sheds that smell of clove and ginger.
ev.aden.a.choice.ask-routes: Ask the camel-masters which roads leave the harbour
ev.aden.a.choice.buy-pepper: Buy a sack of Malabar pepper for the onward road
ev.aden.a.choice.walk: Walk the sheds and watch the lighters load
ev.aden.a.title: The Pepper Lighters and the Camel Road
ev.aden.b.body: Above the harbour rises the Soldan's mosque, where the Saracens of Aden gather at the hours of prayer. Below it, the customs clerks take their due on every bale that crosses the mole — a tenth on pepper, a fee on cloth and dates. The harbour-master keeps a register in Arabic script; no ship departs without his seal. You mark how the muezzin's call and the clerks' abacus share the same wind off the sea.
ev.aden.b.choice.listen-prayer: Listen at the mosque door as the Soldan's men pray
ev.aden.b.choice.observe: Stand aside and observe the customs at the mole
ev.aden.b.choice.pay-frankincense: Pay the harbour fee and buy frankincense from a Somali trader
ev.aden.b.title: The Soldan's Mosque and the Harbour Customs
ev.aden.entry.body: You must know that in the province of ADEN there is a Prince who is called the Soldan. The people are all Saracens and adorers of Mahommet, and have a great hatred of Christians. There are many towns and villages in the country. This Aden is the port to which many of the ships of India come with their cargoes; and from this haven the merchants carry the goods a distance of seven days further in small vessels. At the end of those seven days they land the goods and load them on camels, and so carry them a land journey of 30 days. This brings them to the river of ALEXANDRIA, and by it they descend to the latter city. It is by this way through Aden that the Saracens of Alexandria receive all their stores of pepper and other spicery; and there is no other route equally good and convenient by which these goods could reach that place.
ev.aden.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzā without delay
ev.aden.entry.title: Concerning the Province of Aden
ev.alexandria.entry.body: You come into Alexandria by the sea-gate of Misr, and the first thing you mark is the weighing of bales. The Sultan's clerks take their tamghā on every pack that leaves the quay — pepper of India, glass of Syria, grain of Egypt, woolens of the Franks. The old light-tower that once guided ships from every sea is a ruin; its stones have gone into the walls. And yet the harbours still teem, and learned men keep cells in this city — imāms and sheikhs whose names are known from Sindia to China. You must know that no junk puts in here without passing beneath the clerks' brushes, and no traveller leaves without hearing what the saints of this place have said of the road ahead.
ev.alexandria.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.alexandria.entry.title: Arriving at Alexandria
ev.alexandria.mentor_geomancy.body: Near the warehouses a geomancer casts for risk on the sea lanes and the desert posts alike.
ev.alexandria.mentor_geomancy.choice.ask: Ask what Populus means for a voyage
ev.alexandria.mentor_geomancy.title: Sand by the Pharos road
ev.antiochia.entry.body: You come down to Antioch upon the river El Aāsī, which the men of Hamah call the Rebel. The town sits under the mountains of the frontier, between Muslim lands and the castles of the Franks that once held this coast. Within the walls is the tomb of Habīb El Najār, which pilgrims visit; beyond, toward the high places, lie the fortresses of the Ismāīlīah — Bugrās, El Shaghar, Masyāf, El Kahf — and no stranger walks freely among them. Caravans still pass the Orontes bridge with silk and steel; the Sultan's watch holds the gates. You must know that this was once among the great cities of the Romans, and men still speak of it as they speak of old Damascus.
ev.antiochia.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.antiochia.entry.title: Arriving at Antiochia
ev.axuma.entry.body: You come into Axum by the highland road, where the air is thin and the stone of the old stelae catches the sun. This was once a Christian kingdom that traded ivory and gold to the Red Sea — you must know that its kings struck coin and sent embassies as far as Constantinople. The Church still prays in Ge'ez within walls of cut stone; the obelisks stand crooked but unbroken. Yet Aden and the Yemeni ports have drawn the sea-trade away, and the bāzār shows more dust than silk. Pilgrims and a few caravans still pause here for water and for the blessing of the priests.
ev.axuma.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.axuma.entry.title: Arriving at Axuma
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.body: Misr and Cairo stand upon the Nile, one city and yet two — the old settlement of Fustāt and the new quarters under the citadel. Four congregational mosques of superb build rise among many lesser ones; the mosque of ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās draws a daily income for its readers and imāms. Theological colleges throughout Misr and Cairo are maintained by the Sultan's bounty — two thousand Egyptian dīnārs a month, men say. Villages and towns follow continuously along the river. You must know that this is the seat of Ayyubid power in Egypt, and that no stranger lodges long without hearing the Friday khutbah in the Sunni manner.
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.title: Arriving at Babylonia Cairus
ev.badashan.a.body: You climb to the highland bāzār where rough lapis lazuli and balas rubies change hands under the king's seal. The stones are dug in great caves among the mountains — men say only the mountain of Syghinan yields the rubies, and that none may carry them beyond the kingdom on pain of forfeiture. Brokers weigh each block on brass scales and murmur prices in a tongue you scarcely follow.
ev.badashan.a.choice.ask-mines: Ask where the ruby mines lie in the mountains
ev.badashan.a.choice.buy-lapis: Buy a block of raw lapis lazuli
ev.badashan.a.choice.walk: Walk among the stone brokers and listen to their bargaining
ev.badashan.a.title: The Lapis and Balas Ruby Trade
ev.badashan.b.body: In the audience hall of Badashan you hear how every prince of the royal blood claims descent from Alexander and the daughter of Darius, Lord of Persia. They call themselves Zulcarniaim in the Saracen tongue — that is to say, Alexander — out of reverence for the great conqueror. The common folk speak a mountain tongue unlike any Arabic or Persian you have heard on the plains. A court scribe writes your name in their script and smiles at your puzzlement.
ev.badashan.b.choice.buy-ruby: Buy a small balas ruby from a licensed broker
ev.badashan.b.choice.learn-tongue: Pay a scribe to teach you a few words of the mountain tongue
ev.badashan.b.choice.listen: Listen as the court herald recites the royal genealogy
ev.badashan.b.title: The Royal Lineage and the Mountain Tongue
ev.badashan.entry.body: Badashan is a Province inhabited by people who worship Mahommet, and have a peculiar language. It forms a very great kingdom, and the royalty is hereditary. All those of the royal blood are descended from King Alexander and the daughter of King Darius, who was Lord of the vast Empire of Persia. And all these kings call themselves in the Saracen tongue ZULCARNIAIN, which is as much as to say _Alexander_; and this out of regard for Alexander the Great. It is in this province that those fine and valuable gems the Balas Rubies are found. They are got in certain rocks among the mountains, and in the search for them the people dig great caves underground, just as is done by miners for silver. There is but one special mountain that produces them, and it is called SYGHINAN. The stones are dug on the king’s account, and no one else dares dig in that mountain on pain of forfeiture of life as well as goods; nor may any one carry the stones out of the kingdom.
ev.badashan.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzeh without delay
ev.badashan.entry.title: Of the Province of Badashan
ev.balc.a.body: Balc was once the mother of cities — the capital of Bactria, where Alexander the Great took Roxana of Sogdiana as his bride. Its walls enclosed more ground than any city in Asia, and its temples held treasure from India, Persia, and Greece. Now its broken ramparts, collapsed domes, and empty palaces tell the same story as every city east of the Oxus: the Mongol rider came, and nothing was left standing. Yet the caravans still stop here, and the city is slowly rebuilding from the rubble. The new houses are smaller, built from the stones of the old, but the market is alive again. The King of Balc pays tribute to the Great Kaan, and the trade of lapis lazuli, rubies, and Turkoman horses keeps the city's heart beating.
ev.balc.a.choice.explore: Search the ruins where Alexander married Roxana
ev.balc.a.choice.fragment: Pick up a carved stone from the old city
ev.balc.a.choice.listen: Ask an old man what this city was in its height
ev.balc.a.title: The Ruins of Bactra
ev.balc.b.body: The caravanserai of Balc is one of the largest on the Silk Road — a fortress-sized courtyard ringed with stables for a thousand camels, storerooms stacked with bales of silk and leather sacks of lapis, and chambers for merchants of every nation. Lapis lazuli from the mines of Badakhshan, which lies twelve days east, is the city's chief treasure; it is sold in rough blocks and traded for silver, silk, and spices. Balas rubies from the mountains fetch prices that would buy a ship in Venice. Horses from the Turkoman plains are auctioned in the inner courtyard. The caravanserai never sleeps; fires burn in the arcades all night, and the smell of lamb kebab and saffron rice hangs in the air.
ev.balc.b.choice.lapis: Buy a block of raw lapis lazuli from Badakhshan
ev.balc.b.choice.ruby: Buy a balas ruby — worth a ship in Venice
ev.balc.b.choice.talk_traders: Ask the caravan masters where the roads go
ev.balc.b.title: The Caravanserai of Balc
ev.balc.c.body: On a hill outside the city, a fire-temple of the ancient Persian faith still burns — the Magi tend a flame they say has never been extinguished since the days of Zoroaster, a thousand years before the Prophet. The people call it the Tomb of the Magi, and they say that the three wise men who visited the infant Christ are buried here, in three stone sarcophagi that still bear traces of gold leaf. Pilgrims from Persia, India, and even distant Cathay climb the hill to leave offerings of incense and silver coins. The Magi in their white robes chant the ancient hymns at dawn and dusk. They say that a man who sleeps at the shrine will dream of his own death — and that every dream they have recorded has come true.
ev.balc.c.choice.chant: Listen to the Magi chant at dawn
ev.balc.c.choice.offering: Leave incense at the fire that has never gone out
ev.balc.c.choice.sleep: Sleep at the Tomb of the Magi and wait for a dream
ev.balc.c.title: The Shrine of the Magi
ev.balc.entry.body: Balc is a noble city and a great, though it was much greater in former days. But the Tartars and other nations have greatly ravaged and destroyed it. There were formerly many fine palaces and buildings of marble, and the ruins of them still remain. The people of the city tell that it was here that Alexander took to wife the daughter of Darius. Here, you should be told, is the end of the empire of the Tartar Lord of the Levant. And this city is also the limit of Persia in the direction between east and north-east. Now, let us quit this city, and I will tell you of another country called DOGANA. When you have quitted the city of which I have been speaking, you ride some 12 days between north-east and east, without finding any human habitation, for the people have all taken refuge in fastnesses among the mountains, on account of the Banditti and armies that harassed them. There is plenty of water on the road, and abundance of game; there are lions too. You can get no provisions on the road, and must carry with you all that you require for these 12 days.
ev.balc.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the bājgāh (toll-house)
ev.balc.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.balc.entry.title: Of the City of Balc
ev.balc.mentor_closure.body: Before you leave Balc, the old copyist of the lapis road asks what you have learned from Balc. The lesson is not a spell or a bargain; it is a way of noticing which detail will matter after the road turns.
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask what the road will demand
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_1_result: The choice leaves a mark: the people of Balc now remember you among the ruins and the lapis road.
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_2: Stay for a day and listen to the whole account
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_2_result: The matter is not finished, but the next road is clear; your name travels ahead with the ruins and the lapis road.
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_3: Thank the guide and keep moving
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_3_result: You close the matter for now. The sign you gained will still guide your next action in Balc.
ev.balc.mentor_closure.title: The Guide of Balc
ev.baldacum.a.body: The great palace of the Caliph of Baghdad covered more ground than any building in Islam. Its golden dome could be seen three days' journey away across the flat plain of the Tigris. Within were halls hung with silk embroidered with gold thread, gardens watered by channels drawn from the river, courtyards paved with marble brought from every corner of the Caliphate, and the treasury that held the tribute of a hundred nations. The Caliph himself was never seen except by a handful of servants and his vizier. His harem contained a thousand women; his guard was an army of twenty thousand Turkic slaves. And yet when Hulagu came to the walls, all that gold and all those swords could not save him.
ev.baldacum.a.choice.explore: Explore the ruined halls of the Caliph
ev.baldacum.a.choice.listen: Hire a guard to tell you what this place once was
ev.baldacum.a.choice.treasure: Bribe the old warden and search the treasury rubble
ev.baldacum.a.title: The Caliph's Palace
ev.baldacum.b.body: Merchants from India, Persia, Syria, and the Levant crowd the covered markets of Baudas. The bazaars are organized by trade — the silversmiths in one vaulted lane, the silk-merchants in another, the spice-sellers in a third — and each guild maintains its own mosque, bathhouse, and coffee-house. Silk and cloth of gold from Mosul, spices from Hormuz and India, pearls from the Gulf, paper from Samarcand, and Damascus steel blades change hands by the hour. The money-changers sit cross-legged behind low tables covered with mountains of silver dirhams; the merchants drink sherbet cooled with snow brought down from the Kurdish mountains and argue over fractions of a grain of gold.
ev.baldacum.b.choice.brocade: Buy a length of Baghdad brocade worked with gold
ev.baldacum.b.choice.sherbet: Drink sherbet with the money-changers and listen
ev.baldacum.b.choice.spices: Ask the spice-sellers where their wares come from
ev.baldacum.b.title: The Bazaars of Baudas
ev.baldacum.c.body: The story of how Hulagu took this city is still told in the bazaars. The Caliph, trusting in his gold and his twenty thousand guards, refused to pay tribute to the Great Khan and defied the Mongol envoy. Hulagu marched on the city with a host that blackened the plain from horizon to horizon. He broke the dikes of the Tigris and flooded the Mongol camp, but his engineers diverted the water and drained the Caliph's moat. When the walls fell, Hulagu shut the Caliph in his own treasury — a tower full of gold, silver, jewels, and silk — and told him to eat his treasure. The Caliph starved among his wealth, and the city burned for a month.
ev.baldacum.c.choice.listen: Hear the full tale of how Hulagu took the city
ev.baldacum.c.choice.record: Write down the story while it is still told
ev.baldacum.c.choice.search: Search for a coin from before the sack
ev.baldacum.c.title: The Fall of the City
ev.baldacum.entry.body: Baudas is a great city, which used to be the seat of the Calif of all the Saracens in the world, just as Rome is the seat of the Pope of all the Christians.
